Read at source 2026-09-30: full text on SciELO (HTML) and the publisher PDF (10.1590/S1984-82502015000400016, pp. 901-909; no PubMed record, so the DOI is the identifier; Crossref title matches verbatim). THE TRIAL MEASURED NO WRINKLES: Corneometer CM 825 (stratum corneum water), Cutometer SEM 575 (Ua/Uf, Ur/Ue, Uv/Ue, Ur/Uf; only Uv/Ue and Ur/Uf are plotted, Figs 6-7) and Reviscometer RV600 (RRTM max, min, medium; anisotropy = max/min, Figs 2-5), on the cheeks and ventral forearms. So the H1, answer and keyword follow the paper's own question (skin mechanics), not 'argireline for wrinkles'. Lead's decisions 2026-09-30: handle renamed from argireline-wrinkle-trial-tadini-2015; primary keyword 'acetyl hexapeptide-3' (Ads 320 US / 50 GB; the paper's own name; no page owns it), secondary 'does argireline tighten skin'; grade A- (blinding not described, indirect measure). 'Older INCI name' rests on tertiary sources (Wikipedia 'Acetyl hexapeptide-3', supplier pages); no Lubrizol or CosIng document read. Design: 40 healthy women 35-55, Fitzpatrick II-IV, non-smokers; forearms within-subject (Argireline cream one arm, vehicle the other); face between groups (half Argireline, half vehicle); 'Applications sites were randomized'; blinding, drop-outs and adverse events not reported. Vehicle: emulsion with glycerin, propylene glycol, octyl octanoate, dimethicone, 7.5% UVA/UVB filter blend, Phenonip; +/- 10% Argireline ('solution containing 0.05% acetyl hexapeptide-3'), so ~0.005% peptide in the cream (our arithmetic, trial cream only). 1.0 mL twice daily; visits baseline, 2 wk, 4 wk, 10-15 h after last application, 30 min at 20 +/- 2 C, 45-60% RH. Stats: Kruskal-Wallis (anisotropy), ANOVA (others), Mann-Whitney / unpaired t at 4 wk vehicle vs peptide; significance p < 0.05 (PDF; the HTML drops the symbol); no exact p-values anywhere. RESULTS: face anisotropy (Fig 5B) significantly below baseline at wk 2 and wk 4 with Argireline, and below vehicle at wk 4; vehicle no significant change. Plotted means extracted from the PDF vector geometry (axis 0-3.5): Argireline 2.49 -> 1.57 (wk 2) -> 1.66 (wk 4); vehicle 2.51 -> 1.97 -> 2.15; shown on the page to one decimal with '≈' (2.5 -> 1.6 -> 1.7; 2.5 -> 2.0 -> 2.2). 'About a third' = 2.49 -> 1.66 is -33% (wk 2: -37%). Forearm anisotropy (5A) no significant change. RRTM max/min/medium (Figs 2-4) no significant change on either site; face RRTM max baseline differed between groups (~232 Argireline vs ~307 vehicle) but the anisotropy baselines matched (2.49 vs 2.51). Hydration (Fig 1): face up with BOTH creams vs baseline (p < 0.01) and held to wk 4; forearm upward trend, p > 0.05; peptide did not add to hydration vs vehicle. Cutometer: no significant change, either site. Authors: lower anisotropy 'suggests increased firmness or tensor effect'; anisotropy rises with age (citing Ruvolo 2007, Hermanns-Le 2001). Funding FAPESP; 'no conflict of interest'; peptide 'kindly provided by Galena Quimica e Farmaceutica Ltda, Campinas' (a Brazilian ingredient fractionator/distributor, galena.com.br). Register corrections: randomisation of application sites IS stated; 'none reported' for adverse events means the paper is silent, not that it reports zero; face comparison is between groups, forearms within-subject; hydration rise on the face only (forearm n.s.). Ethics approval CEP/FCFRP 60/2005.

h1.en: Does Argireline® firm and tighten facial skin?

deck.en: A vehicle-controlled university trial of 10% Argireline® (acetyl hexapeptide-3) on the faces and forearms of 40 women, measured with three skin instruments — read at source, appraised in full.

byline.en: Appraised by the Skingenetix research team. Medically reviewed by Dr Esther Bodde, Cosmetic & Medical Physician. Last reviewed 30 September 2026.

definition.en: Acetyl hexapeptide-3, the name this paper uses, is another label name for acetyl hexapeptide-8 (ingredient lists show both): the peptide sold as [Argireline®](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/acetyl-hexapeptide-8-research), made by Lipotec, now part of Lubrizol, and widely used for the look of expression lines. Skin anisotropy, the measure that changed in this trial, compares how fast a tiny sound pulse crosses the skin in different directions; the gap widens as skin ages.

answer.en: The Tadini 2015 trial tested a cream with 10% Argireline® (acetyl hexapeptide-3) against the same cream without it in 40 women aged 35 to 55. On the face, only the Argireline cream significantly lowered anisotropy, a firmness-related measure that rises with age: by about a third within two weeks, and below the plain cream at four weeks (p < 0.05).

verdict.en: **Our verdict:** a publicly funded university trial that measured how facial skin behaves rather than how lines look. With 10% Argireline®, facial anisotropy fell by about a third within two weeks and stayed down, which the authors read as firmer, tauter skin; the plain cream made no significant change. We read it beside the two Argireline® wrinkle trials.

seo_title.en: Tadini 2015: Does Acetyl Hexapeptide-3 Firm Skin?

seo_description.en: In a vehicle-controlled trial of 40 women, 10% Argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-3) cut a firmness measure of facial skin by about a third in 2 weeks.

label.en: Firmness signal on the face by week 4

note.en: Facial anisotropy, which rises as skin loses firmness, fell from about 2.5 to 1.7 with Argireline® and was lower than with the plain cream at week 4 (p < 0.05); the plain cream's own change was not significant. Group means read from Figure 5B ([Tadini et al., 2015](https://doi.org/10.1590/S1984-82502015000400016)).
Two weeks in, facial anisotropy on the Argireline® cream was already significantly below its start, at about 1.6, and it stayed down at the week-4 visit.

label.en: Women, in a publicly funded trial (one measure had a size of effect)

note.en: A University of São Paulo trial funded by the São Paulo Research Foundation, with no conflicts of interest declared: the only one of our three appraised Argireline® trials to name a public funder.

v.en: Vehicle-controlled, with application sites assigned at random: each woman used both creams on her forearms, one per arm; on the face, half the women used each cream.
40 healthy women aged 35 to 55, skin types II to IV on the Fitzpatrick scale (fair to light brown), non-smokers.
1 mL of a cream with UVA/UVB filters and 10% Argireline®, twice a day, to the whole face or one inner forearm.
The same cream without Argireline®: on the other forearm, and on the faces of the other half of the group.
4 weeks, measured at the start, at week 2 and at week 4.
On the cheeks and inner forearms: a Corneometer CM 825 for surface moisture, a Cutometer SEM 575 for elasticity and a Reviscometer RV600 for anisotropy.
10% Argireline®, which the paper describes as a solution containing 0.05% acetyl hexapeptide-3: about 0.005% peptide in the cream, and the same 10% as the other two Argireline® trials.

Publicly funded (FAPESP, the São Paulo Research Foundation) and run at the University of São Paulo; no conflicts declared. Galena Química e Farmacêutica, a Brazilian ingredient distributor, donated the peptide.
A− — controlled, instrument-measured and publicly funded (FAPESP); blinding is not described, and the positive result is a firmness-related measure rather than a wrinkle measurement.

title.en: Facial skin anisotropy over four weeks

subtitle.en: Slowest ÷ fastest time for a sound pulse to cross the cheek skin (Reviscometer). Lower means the skin behaves more evenly in every direction; it rises with age. Group means read from Figure 5B.

caption.en: With 10% Argireline®, facial anisotropy fell from about 2.5 to about 1.6 at week 2 and 1.7 at week 4: significantly below the start at both visits, and below the plain cream at week 4 (p < 0.05). On the plain cream it went from about 2.5 to about 2.2, not a significant change (Tadini et al., 2015).

alt.en: A glass pipette releasing a single clear droplet onto a pale grey surface

body.en: Forty healthy women aged 35 to 55 applied a cream with UVA/UVB filters twice a day for four weeks, with or without 10% Argireline®. Each put the Argireline® version on one inner forearm and the plain version on the other; on the face, half the women used each. Application sites were assigned at random, and no other skincare was allowed on the test areas.

At the start, week 2 and week 4, after 30 minutes' rest in a room at about 20 °C, the team measured the cheeks and forearms: moisture with a Corneometer, elasticity with a Cutometer, which draws the skin up by gentle suction, and anisotropy with a Reviscometer, which times a tiny sound pulse across the skin in several directions.

items.en: What was measured. The positive result is on anisotropy, a Reviscometer reading that rises as skin ages. With Argireline® it fell on the face, which the authors read as firmer, tauter skin. The trial measured firmness, elasticity and moisture; the wrinkle trials measured lines.

What moved and what held. Facial anisotropy fell significantly with Argireline® by week 2 and stayed lower at week 4, when it was also significantly lower than with the plain cream. The suction-based elasticity readings held steady on both creams, as did the separate direction timings behind the anisotropy ratio.

Moisture rose with both creams. Facial moisture rose with the Argireline® cream and with the plain cream alike (p < 0.01 against the start) and stayed up for four weeks, so the moisture gain belongs to the base cream; the firmness change was the peptide's own.

Face, not forearm. The changes were on the face; on the inner forearm, neither cream changed anisotropy or elasticity significantly. The authors point out that facial skin sees more sun and responds more to anti-ageing products.

How the groups compare. On the face, the comparison is between two groups of women, who started with almost identical anisotropy (about 2.5 each). The paper does not describe blinding, drop-outs or side effects, and it reports significance at p < 0.05 without exact values; the figures on this page are read from its Figure 5B.

Who paid. FAPESP, São Paulo's public research foundation, funded the work, and the authors declared no conflicts. Galena Química e Farmacêutica, a Brazilian ingredient distributor, donated the Argireline®.

heading.en: Where this trial sits in the evidence

body.en: Three controlled trials have tested 10% Argireline® on skin, and each measured something different. Around the eyes, clinicians graded 22 of 45 people clearly improved after four weeks, against none of 15 on placebo ([Wang et al., 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23417317/); our [crow's-feet appraisal](https://www.skingenetix.com/blogs/clinical-studies/argireline-crows-feet-trial-wang-2013)). On the forehead, roughness fell 7.4% by day 20 while it rose 4.3% on placebo ([Raikou et al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.1111/jocd.12314); our [forehead appraisal](https://www.skingenetix.com/blogs/clinical-studies/argireline-forehead-roughness-trial-raikou-2017)).

This is the trial that measured how the skin itself behaves, and the only one of the three with a named public funder. All three point the same way: facial skin measured better with Argireline® than without it, within weeks, at 10%. People sometimes ask whether Argireline® can loosen skin; in this trial, elasticity held steady and the one measure that changed moved towards firmer skin.

Every study we rely on, graded, is on the [Argireline® evidence hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/acetyl-hexapeptide-8-research), alongside our other [ingredient research](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/the-science), and the [Clinical studies](https://www.skingenetix.com/blogs/clinical-studies) list gathers every trial we have appraised.

answers.en: It shows that a cream with 10% Argireline® changed a firmness-related measure of facial skin within two weeks: anisotropy fell by about a third and, at four weeks, was significantly lower than with the same cream without the peptide (p < 0.05). It measured firmness rather than lines; the wrinkle trials, and every other study, are on the [Argireline® evidence hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/acetyl-hexapeptide-8-research).

10% Argireline®, which the paper describes as a solution containing 0.05% acetyl hexapeptide-3, so the finished cream held about 0.005% of the peptide itself. That is the same 10% level used in the crow's-feet and forehead trials, at the top of the 2–10% range its maker recommends.

It is the only Argireline® trial we appraise that names a public funder: a University of São Paulo study, funded by FAPESP, the São Paulo Research Foundation, and published in the peer-reviewed Brazilian Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences, with no conflicts of interest declared. The peptide was donated by Galena Química e Farmacêutica, a Brazilian ingredient distributor.

Our [Acetyl Hexapeptide-8 Serum](https://www.skingenetix.com/products/acetyl-hexapeptide-8-anti-wrinkle-serum) lists 10% Argireline®, the level used in this trial, applied the same way, twice a day. It is a different formula from the trial's cream, so its results are not the trial's results: we cite this trial as evidence for the ingredient as studied.

heading.en: What it means for our products

body.en: This trial adds something the wrinkle trials do not: a publicly funded, instrument-measured sign that 10% Argireline® changes how facial skin behaves. Within two weeks, the skin responded more evenly in every direction, which the authors read as firmer skin.

Our [Acetyl Hexapeptide-8 Serum](https://www.skingenetix.com/products/acetyl-hexapeptide-8-anti-wrinkle-serum) lists the same 10% Argireline®. It is a different formula from the trial's cream, so we cite the trial for the ingredient as studied, not as a result our serum has repeated. The rest of the evidence is on the [Argireline® research hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/acetyl-hexapeptide-8-research).
